prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: My opening first choice was B002 (flocking), and I still regard it as the deepest conceptual contribution on the shortlist. But on reading the full set of ballots I move the optical lattice clock to the top of my preferred configuration. Five of eight members place it in their top three, and the reasons given are independent of one another and robust: Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a concrete, original invention with a clear before and after; Ye's group took it to the 1e-18 regime and made it a general tool; many laboratories reproduce and now surpass the performance; and it feeds directly into tests of relativistic time dilation, searches for variation of constants and the pending redefinition of the second. The two-name attribution is unusually clean, with no obvious principal missing from the supplied credit, which matters more to me after reading how many of the other candidates are compromised by omitted names. A statistical-physics colleague should say plainly that a measurement-science prize is not lesser science: the many-body, spin-polarised Fermi-gas operation of the clock is itself a statistical-physics result.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the clock is an instrument-level advance on a field already honoured in 2005 (frequency combs and precision spectroscopy) and in 2012 and 1997 (ion traps and laser cooling), so one can argue that the committee would be rewarding an incremental extension of a recently recognised line of work. The headline application, the redefinition of the SI second, has not happened yet, and the fundamental-physics payoffs (dark matter, varying constants) are still prospective rather than realised. Against my own first choice, B002 has far thinner opening support (one first place, no further top-three ranking), quantitative confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is limited, and priority questions for early alignment-dynamics work are not settled by the supplied credit, so I cannot honestly claim it is ready to win a prize this year on the strength of the ballots alone.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B027 first and B057 second, arguing that the lattice clock is a concrete invention with no obvious missing principal and that topological insulators are original, clear and broadly influential.
responses.response: I agree on B027 and have moved towards it for exactly the attribution reason he gives. On B057 I am more cautious than he is: his own ballot notes that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Hasan and Cava, are absent from the supplied credit, and the 2016 prize already covered topological phases of matter. The conceptual weight is real, but I do not think a three-name credit that leaves out the proposers of the HgTe experiment is cleaner than the clock, so I keep B057 as an alternative rather than my preferred choice.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B027 first as a clean, original instrument-level invention in laser spectroscopy, with independent laboratories agreeing at the 1e-18 level, and ranks atom interferometry B032 third.
responses.response: I agree that the independent agreement at 1e-18 across several national laboratories is what separates the clock from many other candidates: it is a result that has already been cross-checked by people with no stake in the original claim. Where I differ is on B032. His own attribution paragraph concedes that the credit is complicated by Chu and by the early Ramsey-Borde work, and I would not let a messy three-way attribution compete with a two-name prize that is clean. I would take B032 only if the committee wanted a second metrology part, and I do not see a need for one.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube B041 first on the grounds that it opened a new observational window and founded neutrino astronomy, and puts B027 second, with B014 (twisted bilayer graphene) fourth and flagged as possibly premature.
responses.response: I take the discovery argument for IceCube seriously and I do not equate it with the clock simply because more members ranked the clock highly. My reservation is attribution: the diffuse-flux discovery is a large-collaboration result, and Pearce's own ballot admits that a two-person credit is only defensible, with the instrument and the physics inseparable. That is a harder prize to word fairly than the clock. I would not oppose B041 in a configuration that carries a fair citation, but I do not rank it above B027. I agree with his caution on B014, where the mechanism of the correlated and superconducting phases is still disputed.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B027 first, stressing centimetre-scale tests of relativistic time dilation and sensitivity to variation of constants and dark matter, and ranks B057 second as arguably overdue after 2016.
responses.response: I agree with her emphasis on the measurable tests, and I would put the citation in terms of the invention rather than its applications, so the committee does not commit to the second-redefinition outcome. I disagree gently with the view that B057 is overdue: a field being fifteen years old and stable is a reason for maturity, but the 2016 prize and the unsettled credit for the HgTe proposal and the three-dimensional materials argue for care, not urgency.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory B054 first as a systematically improvable framework used across correlated materials, while noting that Walter Metzner is missing from the supplied credit.
responses.response: As a theorist I sympathise with the case for B054, and I accept that the method is mature and widely used. But he identifies the central difficulty himself: the infinite-dimension limit is Metzner and Vollhardt's step, and a prize that omits Metzner, with a cap of three laureates, would be structurally unfair. I do not think the committee can fix that by adjusting the citation, so I do not support B054 as my preferred prize this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the optical lattice clock as a sufficiently new step after the 2005, 2012 and 1997 recognitions of closely related precision-measurement and laser-cooling work.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second should affect timing, either as a reason to wait or as a reason to act now.

Whether flocking (B002) can be given a clean attribution between the Vicsek model and the Toner-Tu hydrodynamic theory, and whether the exponent confirmations are strong enough; I am recalling the experimental status from memory.
Whether a two-part prize pairing B027 with a theory candidate is possible within three names; with B002 at three credited names it is not, so I have not proposed it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My documented co-authors and institutions (Fulde, Gustavsson, Wilkinson, Einarsson, Candelier, Pumir, Meibohm; Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg, Gothenburg) do not include any credited name on the shortlist. I do note an intellectual proximity, not a personal tie, to active matter (B002) and to stochastic processes, which is why I have deliberately not made B002 my preferred configuration on my opening preference alone.
